title: Morning Edition
dek: The U.S.–Iran pause breaks down around Hormuz, an international court challenges India’s suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty, Libya’s rivals sign an election roadmap, and Iceland decides against reopening EU accession talks.

lead_story.headline: The U.S.–Iran pause has broken down around the Strait of Hormuz
lead_story.summary: U.S. forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island after U.S. Central Command said Revolutionary Guard units were preparing rockets carrying sea mines for the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded with missiles and drones aimed at U.S. bases in Jordan; Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles. The exchange was the first known direct U.S. strike on Iran since late July and follows only days after tentative work on a navigation framework for the strait.
lead_story.why_it_matters: This is the material breakdown that recent Morning Editions were waiting for before returning to Hormuz. A renewed cycle of strikes near the world’s most important oil chokepoint can affect shipping, energy prices and several neighboring states even if neither side intends a wider war. Early Iranian damage claims remain unverified, so the clearest facts are the strikes themselves, the attempted retaliation and the interception reports.

items.headline: An arbitration court says India cannot suspend the Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan
items.summary: The Permanent Court of Arbitration said the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and ordered India to observe treaty limits while a World Bank-appointed neutral expert reviews contested hydropower designs in Kashmir. India, which suspended participation after a 2025 attack in Kashmir, rejected the ruling and says the tribunal has no jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions.
items.why_it_matters: The treaty has survived wars because both countries depend on a predictable river system. The ruling therefore matters even if enforcement is contested: it sharpens the legal conflict over whether a state can suspend a long-running water treaty during a security crisis and raises the stakes around dams on rivers vital to Pakistani agriculture.

items.headline: Libya’s rival institutions signed a roadmap aimed at national elections within two years
items.summary: A UN-facilitated agreement signed in Tripoli covers the first two steps of a new political roadmap: reconstituting the national election commission and resolving constitutional and legal rules for presidential and legislative elections. The parties committed to work toward elections within 24 months under a unified executive, while the House of Representatives and High State Council are supposed to validate the framework within one month.
items.why_it_matters: Libya has spent years with rival governments, overlapping institutions and repeatedly delayed elections. This agreement is not a settlement by itself, but it creates specific institutional tasks, deadlines and a follow-up mechanism that can be judged against actual implementation rather than another open-ended promise of elections.

items.headline: Iceland voted 52.8% to 47.2% against reopening EU accession talks
items.summary: Final results from Iceland’s referendum show a narrow national majority against restarting European Union membership negotiations. The result was sharply geographic: Reykjavík backed reopening talks while every other constituency voted no. The government has said it will respect the outcome and not restart negotiations during its current term.
items.why_it_matters: The vote was not on EU membership itself, but it closes the most immediate path toward accession and shows how sovereignty, fisheries and Arctic security are pulling Iceland in different directions. Iceland will remain deeply integrated with Europe through the European Economic Area and Schengen while staying outside EU decision-making.

items.headline: Africa’s diesel supply chain is shifting from the Middle East toward Asia
items.summary: Ship-tracking and trade data indicate that Asia, including India, will send roughly 1.8–2.0 million metric tons of diesel to Africa in August, the highest level in at least four and a half years. Middle Eastern shipments are estimated at only 600,000–800,000 tons, their lowest in almost nine years, as the Iran war, Red Sea risks and reduced Saudi refinery output disrupt established routes.
items.why_it_matters: Fuel supply chains are adapting around conflict in real time. Africa historically sourced about half of its imported diesel from the Middle East; replacing those barrels from much farther east can keep fuel available, but it also changes freight costs, refinery incentives and exposure to Asian supply conditions. This is a concrete example of geopolitical disruption becoming ordinary economic infrastructure.

items.headline: Footprints in Kenya suggest Paranthropus boisei could be much larger—and more social—than its bones implied
items.summary: A PNAS study of roughly 1.4-million-year-old trackways near Lake Turkana attributes a set of footprints to eight Paranthropus boisei individuals moving across the same lakeshore surface. Track size suggests some individuals may have stood around 1.8 metres tall and weighed about 75 kilograms, while the concentration of mostly adult-sized tracks raises the possibility of group travel.
items.why_it_matters: Bones preserve anatomy; footprints can preserve behavior over a very short interval. These tracks therefore offer an unusually direct glimpse of body size and social movement in a hominin known mostly from skulls and teeth. The species assignment and social interpretation are reasoned reconstructions rather than certainties, so they should be treated as strong hypotheses rather than a photograph of a known social system.
items.source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

worth_your_time.headline: Africa writes back
worth_your_time.summary: D Vance Smith follows the history of Libyco-Berber writing across North Africa to show how European scholars repeatedly mistook missing archives for missing literacy. The essay moves from ancient inscriptions and colonial collecting to modern Amazigh identity and asks what scholars fail to see when their definitions of writing and knowledge already assume a European path of development.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: It is a durable corrective to a common historical error: absence from familiar archives is not evidence that a society lacked writing, memory or intellectual life. The piece is also about method—how even sympathetic scholarship can reproduce the assumptions it intends to challenge—and pairs well with today’s deliberately broader geographic and linguistic source mix.

editorial_review.filler_check: pass — the edition is deliberately compact. No Science, Technology or U.S. politics section was added because the strongest current candidates did not improve the paper enough to justify space.
editorial_review.repetition_check: pass with two justified returns — Hormuz returns because direct U.S.–Iran strikes are the significant breakdown explicitly identified in the August 27 review as a threshold for renewed coverage. Iceland returns from the August 28 pre-vote item because the referendum now has a verified final result. Turkey–Saudi Arabia–Pakistan, Nepal, Roman, Venezuela, Niger and the yen were left out.
editorial_review.geographic_check: pass — the current-news core spans the Gulf, South Asia, North Africa, the North Atlantic/Europe and an Africa–Asia energy trade route, with no U.S.-domestic story occupying the front page.
editorial_review.language_check: pass — direct French reporting from Tunisie Numérique and direct Icelandic reporting from RÚV meet the non-English discovery target; consequential claims in the lead and water-treaty story were cross-checked through additional regional/international reporting.
editorial_review.discovery_check: pass — the Lake Turkana footprint research and the Libyco-Berber long read supply substantive exploration in paleoanthropology, language and African intellectual history rather than random novelty.
editorial_review.long_read_check: pass — Aeon’s 2021 essay is intentionally evergreen, not a stale current-affairs selection, and is distinct from the recent water-geopolitics, Daoism, economic-security, Enlightenment and technocracy pieces.
editorial_review.ideas_check: pass — no separate Ideas section was forced. The long read carries the reflective material more strongly than the available current opinion pieces.
editorial_review.difference_from_recent: Today moves away from yesterday’s collective-defence pact, Nepal disaster, Roman launch, Brazilian land policy and Greenland glacier ecology. The front page instead centers on a renewed Gulf military exchange, transboundary water law, Libyan institution-building and a completed Icelandic referendum.
notes_for_next_edition: Do not repeat the U.S.–Iran exchange for routine retaliation or market moves; return for a wider regional attack, a sustained new campaign, closure/mining that materially changes Hormuz traffic, or a verified diplomatic settlement.
India–Pakistan water is now in rotation; return only for compliance/noncompliance with the ruling, a neutral-expert decision, major dam operation changes or a new bilateral agreement.

Libya can return if the House of Representatives and High State Council validate or reject the roadmap, the election commission is actually reconstituted, or the unified-executive question produces a consequential break.
Iceland’s EU question should leave rotation unless the government reverses course or the formal application status materially changes.
Continue rotating direct non-English sourcing; French and Icelandic were useful today, so seek strong Arabic, Asian or African-language originals next.
